title: How to Estimate Retirement Spending Using Your Current Lifestyle
description: A bottom-up budgeting approach to replace the '80% Rule'.
content:
The old rule of thumb says you need 80% of your pre-retirement income to maintain your lifestyle. This is a blunt instrument that often leads to over-saving or under-saving. A more accurate method is 'Bottom-Up Budgeting'. By auditing your current spending and adjusting for the specific lifestyle changes of retirement (no commute vs. more travel), you can pinpoint your 'Burn Rate'. This guide helps you convert your current bank statement into a future retirement budget.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Work' Deduction: You spend thousands a year on working. Commuting, professional clothes, lunches out, and retirement contributions all stop. Deduct these.
  • The 'Fun' Addition: You gain 40-50 hours of free time a week. If you fill that with golf or travel, spending goes up. Budget for the 'Go-Go' years.
  • The Healthcare Spike: Pre-65, you pay full insurance premiums. Post-65, you pay Medicare. Model the gap years accurately.
  • Inflation is Personal: Your personal inflation rate depends on your spending. If you own a paid-off home, housing inflation doesn't hurt you. If you rent, it does.

Why It Matters (US Context)

BLS data shows spending follows a 'Smile' curve: high at 65, dipping at 75, and rising at 85 (medical). A static inflation-adjusted budget often overestimates spending in the middle years and underestimates it at the end.

The Adjustment Worksheet

Take your current monthly spend ($5,000). Now adjust.

Subtract (Costs that Vanish)

  • Mortgage: -$1,500 (If paid off by retirement).
  • Savings: -$1,000 (You stop contributing to 401k).
  • FICA Tax: -$400 (No payroll tax on withdrawals).
  • Work Commute: -$200.
  • Net Reduction: -$3,100.

Add (New Costs)

  • Travel: +$800 (2 big trips a year).
  • Healthcare: +$500 (Medicare + Gap + Dental).
  • Hobbies: +$300.
  • Net Addition: +$1,600.

Result: Current Spend $5,000 -> Future Spend $3,500.
Insight: Your 'Replacement Rate' is actually 70%, but the composition is totally different.

Stress Testing

  1. The 'Practice Year': One year before retiring, live on your projected budget. Can you do it? If not, adjust the plan.
  2. The 'Lumpy' Audit: Don't forget car replacements (every 7 years) and home repairs (1% value/year). Add a monthly 'Sinking Fund' line item for these.
  3. Inflation buffer: Assume 3% inflation. But for healthcare, assume 5%. Run two separate inflation rates in your spreadsheet.
  4. Tax Estimate: Remember, $3,500 spendable might require $4,000 gross withdrawal if coming from a Traditional IRA. Don't forget the IRS.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does spending decrease with age?

Yes. From 75 to 85, spending drops significantly (less travel/dining). This is the 'Slow-Go' phase. You might not need to adjust for inflation during this decade.

What about long-term care?

That is a separate 'Catastrophic' bucket. Do not try to fund nursing home care from your monthly grocery budget. Use insurance or home equity.

Should I budget for supporting kids?

If you are currently supporting adults, assume you will continue. 'Economic Outpatient Care' rarely stops just because you retired.
